questions.question: What is Amazon S3 and what type of storage does it provide?
questions.answer: Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is a fully managed, scalable object storage service. Unlike block storage (EBS) attached to servers or file storage (EFS) shared over a network, S3 stores data as objects in containers called buckets. Each object gets a unique URL, making it accessible from anywhere on the internet with the right permissions. AWS manages all hardware — you never worry about disk capacity or server maintenance.

questions.question: What is the difference between a bucket and an object in S3?
questions.answer: A bucket is a top-level container you create in a specific AWS region — like a folder on your computer, but globally accessible. An object is any file you store inside a bucket — an image, a ZIP archive, a log file — anything. Each object has a key (its name/path), metadata, and its actual data. Bucket names must be globally unique across all AWS accounts because the bucket name becomes part of every object's URL.

questions.question: What are the S3 upload size limits?
questions.answer: There are two key limits: the maximum object size is 5 TB — the largest single file S3 can hold. The maximum single PUT upload size is 5 GB — you cannot upload more than 5 GB in one operation. For files larger than 5 GB, you must use Multipart Upload, which splits the file into smaller chunks, uploads them in parallel for speed, and S3 reassembles them as a single object.

questions.question: What is S3 Versioning and what problems does it solve?
questions.answer: S3 Versioning keeps multiple copies of the same object whenever you upload a new version with the same key name. Instead of replacing the old file, S3 creates a new version and assigns it a unique Version ID. This solves two problems: accidental overwrite protection (you can restore any previous version) and accidental deletion protection (deleting an object only adds a delete marker; the versions remain and can be restored).

questions.question: What are S3 storage classes and why do they exist?
questions.answer: Storage classes are types of storage you choose for each object in S3. They exist because not all data needs the same performance or cost level. Frequently accessed data uses S3 Standard (fastest, most expensive). Rarely accessed data can use Standard-IA or Glacier (slower, much cheaper). If you do not know access patterns, Intelligent-Tiering monitors and optimizes automatically. AWS introduced storage classes to help customers pay only for the performance level they actually need.

questions.question: What is the difference between S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA?
questions.answer: Both are designed for infrequently accessed data with millisecond retrieval and a 128 KB minimum billable size. The key difference is resilience: Standard-IA stores data across 3+ Availability Zones for fault tolerance. One Zone-IA stores data in only one AZ, making it about 20% cheaper — but if that AZ fails, data is temporarily or permanently unavailable. Use One Zone-IA only for data that can be recreated if lost, like generated thumbnails.

questions.question: What is a delete marker in S3?
questions.answer: When you delete an object from a versioning-enabled bucket, S3 does not actually delete the data. Instead, it creates a delete marker — a special placeholder that makes the object invisible in the main view. All versions still exist in the versions view. To restore the object, you simply delete the delete marker, and the most recent version reappears in the main view automatically. To permanently delete a specific version, you must explicitly delete it from the versions view.

questions.question: What is the durability guarantee of S3?
questions.answer: S3 guarantees 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability for objects. This means if you store 10 million objects, you can statistically expect to lose at most one object over 10,000 years. AWS achieves this by automatically replicating data across multiple physical devices and multiple facilities within a region. This applies to all S3 storage classes, though One Zone-IA has lower availability (not lower durability) because it uses only one AZ.

questions.question: How does Multipart Upload work?
questions.answer: Multipart Upload breaks a large file into smaller parts (chunks), uploads each part independently and in parallel, then S3 assembles all parts back into the original file. This is required for files over 5 GB and recommended for files over 100 MB. The benefits are speed (parallel uploads), reliability (if one part fails, retry only that part, not the whole file), and the ability to pause and resume uploads. In modern AWS Console and SDKs, this happens automatically for large files.

questions.question: What makes S3 bucket names globally unique?
questions.answer: S3 bucket names must be globally unique across all AWS accounts worldwide because the bucket name is literally embedded in every object's URL. The URL format is https://[bucket-name].s3.[region].amazonaws.com/[key]. Since these URLs must be resolvable from anywhere on the internet, two buckets cannot share the same name — just like two websites cannot share the same domain name.

questions.question: Describe a situation where you would choose Glacier Deep Archive over S3 Standard. Walk through your reasoning.
questions.answer: (Situation) A financial services company needs to retain transaction logs for 10 years to comply with SEC regulations. The logs are never accessed unless an audit is triggered — maybe once every 3–5 years. (Task) Choose the most cost-effective storage class that still meets retrieval requirements. (Action) I recommended Glacier Deep Archive because: the data is effectively frozen (no regular access), retrieval times of up to 12 hours are acceptable for audit scenarios, and the cost is dramatically lower than Standard or even Glacier Flexible. (Result) The company reduced storage costs by over 80% compared to S3 Standard, while staying compliant with their 10-year retention requirement.

questions.question: A user accidentally deleted an important file from S3. How do you recover it?
questions.answer: (Situation) A team member deleted a critical configuration file from S3. The bucket has versioning enabled. (Task) Restore the file without data loss. (Action) I navigated to the bucket, clicked Show Versions to reveal all versions including the delete marker. I selected the delete marker (the entry with the DM badge and no file size) and permanently deleted it. (Result) The most recent version of the file immediately reappeared in the main bucket view, fully restored — no data was lost because versioning preserved all versions and only added a delete marker on deletion.

questions.question: A startup says their storage costs are too high. They store millions of user images and access patterns are unpredictable. What do you recommend?
questions.answer: (Situation) A startup with millions of user images is paying S3 Standard rates for everything but most images are rarely accessed after the first week. (Task) Reduce costs without manual management of individual objects. (Action) I recommended S3 Intelligent-Tiering. It monitors each object's access pattern and automatically moves objects from Frequent Access to Infrequent Access (after 30 days of no access) to Archive tiers (after 90+ days). No retrieval fee applies. They pay a small per-object monitoring fee but save significantly on storage. (Result) The startup reduced storage costs by roughly 40–60% without writing a single lifecycle rule or touching individual objects.

questions.question: A developer uploaded a 200 MB config file with wrong data. The bucket has versioning enabled. How do you roll back to the previous version?
questions.answer: (Situation) A misconfigured 200 MB file was uploaded to S3, overwriting the working configuration. (Task) Restore the previous working version. (Action) In the S3 console, I clicked Show Versions on the bucket. I identified the previous (correct) version by its timestamp and Version ID. I selected that version and downloaded it, then uploaded it again — or alternatively, I could copy it using the AWS CLI with --version-id to promote it as the latest version. (Result) The working configuration was restored without losing any version history. The bad upload still exists as a version but is no longer the latest.

questions.question: Explain when you would use Object Lock Compliance mode vs Governance mode.
questions.answer: (Situation) A healthcare company needs to store patient records for 7 years. A media company needs to protect original video content but wants admins to be able to fix errors. (Task) Choose the right Object Lock mode for each. (Action) For healthcare: Compliance mode — no one, not even root, can delete or modify records until 7 years expire. This is required to satisfy HIPAA regulations. For the media company: Governance mode — content is protected from accidental deletion by regular users, but designated admin users with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission can make corrections when genuinely needed. (Result) Each organization got the level of immutability appropriate to their risk tolerance and regulatory environment.

questions.question: You need to store backup data that must be retrievable within milliseconds even though it is only accessed once a month. Which storage class do you use?
questions.answer: (Situation) A company has disaster recovery backups in S3 accessed monthly but requiring instant retrieval in an emergency. (Task) Choose the most cost-effective class with millisecond access. (Action) I recommended S3 Standard-IA. It stores data across multiple AZs (resilient), provides millisecond access when needed, and costs significantly less than Standard because the data is accessed infrequently. Glacier Instant Retrieval could work for quarterly access but is designed for data accessed even less often. (Result) The company saved on storage costs while keeping the guarantee that backups can be retrieved in milliseconds during a real disaster scenario.

questions.question: Why would you NOT use S3 One Zone-IA for primary database backups?
questions.answer: (Situation) A team proposes using One Zone-IA for all backups to minimize costs. (Task) Evaluate this decision. (Action) I advised against it for primary backups because One Zone-IA stores data in only one Availability Zone. If that AZ suffers a catastrophic failure — which, while rare, is not impossible — the backup data is permanently lost. Backups exist precisely for disaster scenarios, and losing your backup at the same time as your primary data is a catastrophic double failure. (Result) We chose Standard-IA instead — same infrequent access pricing model, multi-AZ resilience, only slightly more expensive, but with the reliability a backup system requires.

questions.question: A customer complains their S3 storage bill is high due to versioning keeping old versions of large files. How do you solve this without disabling versioning?
questions.answer: (Situation) Versioning is accumulating old versions of 10 GB video files, tripling storage costs. (Task) Control versioning storage costs without losing the protection versioning provides. (Action) I configured an S3 Lifecycle Policy on the bucket to automatically transition non-current (old) versions to Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days and permanently expire them after 365 days. This keeps recent versions accessible for fast rollback while moving aging versions to near-zero-cost archive storage, then cleaning them up after a year. (Result) Storage costs dropped significantly while the team retained access to the last 30 days of version history for rollback protection.

questions.question: What is the difference between S3 durability and S3 availability?
questions.answer: (Situation) A team asks whether the 11 nines durability guarantee means S3 will always be accessible. (Task) Clarify the distinction. (Action) I explained: Durability (11 nines = 99.999999999%) means your data will not be lost — AWS replicates it so thoroughly that losing data is statistically near-impossible. Availability (99.99% for S3 Standard, 99.9% for Standard-IA) means the percentage of time the service is accessible — downtime is possible, just extremely rare. You can have high durability but lower availability: your data is safe but temporarily unreachable during an outage. (Result) The team understood they needed both high durability AND high availability for critical workloads, pointing them toward S3 Standard or Multi-Region Access Points.

questions.question: During an investigation, legal holds need to be placed on all S3 objects related to a specific project. How do you implement this?
questions.answer: (Situation) A company receives legal notice requiring preservation of all files related to Project X pending litigation. (Task) Ensure all relevant S3 objects cannot be deleted or modified until the case resolves. (Action) I identified all relevant objects and used the AWS CLI or SDK to apply S3 Object Lock Legal Hold to each one — setting legal hold to ON using s3:PutObjectLegalHold permission. Unlike retention periods, a legal hold has no fixed expiry date. (Result) All Project X files are now legally protected — no one can delete or overwrite them until we explicitly remove the legal hold after the court case concludes, regardless of any bucket-level retention settings.

questions.question: Design an S3 storage architecture for a media company that stores video uploads. Videos are watched frequently for the first 30 days, occasionally for 31–365 days, and almost never after 1 year. Cost optimization is a priority.
questions.answer: The optimal design uses S3 Lifecycle Policies to automate class transitions: Days 0–30: S3 Standard for all newly uploaded videos (frequent access, millisecond delivery, multi-AZ). Days 31–365: Transition to S3 Standard-IA via a lifecycle rule on day 31. Still millisecond retrieval for occasional views, but significantly cheaper. Day 365+: Transition to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Retrieval may take minutes to hours, acceptable for videos rarely viewed. For videos that should be permanently archived (e.g., original raw footage): Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years. Additionally, enable S3 Versioning on the raw upload bucket to protect against accidental deletion of original masters, and use lifecycle rules to expire non-current versions after 90 days to control version storage costs.

questions.question: Compare S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and Deep Archive. When would you use each?
questions.answer: Glacier Instant Retrieval: Archive data accessed roughly quarterly, with millisecond retrieval when needed. 90-day minimum. Use for medical imaging archives or news media where archives are infrequently but urgently retrieved. Glacier Flexible Retrieval: Archive data accessed once or twice a year. Retrieval takes 1–12 hours standard (or 1–5 minutes expedited at extra cost). 90-day minimum. Use for disaster recovery archives or backup data where same-day retrieval is acceptable. Glacier Deep Archive: Lowest-cost tier, data accessed almost never (once every few years). Retrieval takes 12–48 hours. 180-day minimum. Use for legal/compliance data retained 7–10 years, financial records, regulatory archives where retrieval latency is irrelevant.

questions.question: What are the implications of enabling S3 Object Lock at bucket creation vs later?
questions.answer: S3 Object Lock can ONLY be enabled at bucket creation time — it cannot be added to an existing bucket after creation. This is a critical architectural decision: once you decide a bucket will be an immutable/WORM bucket, you must plan for it upfront. Additionally, enabling Object Lock automatically enables versioning (required for Object Lock to function) and versioning cannot be disabled on Object Lock buckets. Implications: if you realize later that a bucket needs Object Lock, you must create a new bucket, migrate all objects, and apply retention settings during migration. This reinforces why storage architecture decisions must be made before deployment, not as an afterthought.

questions.question: Explain S3 Intelligent-Tiering's internal tier structure and when objects move between tiers.
questions.answer: Intelligent-Tiering has up to 5 tiers: Frequent Access Tier (always active, same performance as Standard, no retrieval fee). Infrequent Access Tier (objects not accessed for 30 consecutive days automatically move here, same millisecond retrieval, no retrieval fee). Archive Instant Access Tier (objects not accessed for 90 consecutive days, millisecond retrieval, optional — must be activated). Archive Access Tier (90–180 days of no access, retrieval in hours, optional — must be activated). Deep Archive Access Tier (180+ days of no access, retrieval in 12 hours, optional — must be activated). If an object in any lower tier is accessed, it immediately moves back to the Frequent Access tier. A per-object monitoring fee is charged monthly. There is NEVER a retrieval fee, regardless of which tier the object is in.

questions.question: A new regulation requires all customer PII data stored in S3 to be immutable for 5 years and completely inaccessible (even to developers) after the retention period. How do you design this?
questions.answer: I would use S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode with a 5-year retention period on a dedicated bucket created with Object Lock enabled. Object Lock in Compliance mode prevents ALL users — including the root account — from modifying or deleting objects during the retention period. After 5 years, the retention period expires automatically and objects can then be deleted via a lifecycle policy that expires objects on day 1826 (5 years). For access control during the retention period: S3 bucket policy with Deny conditions on s3:GetObject for all IAM principals except the application service role, combined with VPC endpoints to restrict access to internal networks only. Versioning is automatically enabled by Object Lock. Audit logs via AWS CloudTrail to record all access attempts to the bucket.
